title: Interfacing
description: Connecting a microcontroller to the world: GPIO, LEDs, switches and debouncing, timers, PWM and serial interfaces.

study.title: General-purpose I/O
study.body: Each GPIO pin is set as an **input** or an **output** by a data-direction register. As an output it drives about $V_{OH} \approx V_{DD}$ for a 1 and $V_{OL} \approx 0$ for a 0, and can source or sink only a limited current (typically 5–20 mA per pin). As an input it has a very high impedance and reads the logic level; an unconnected (floating) input reads random values, so every input needs a defined level. Writing or reading the port register sets or reads all pins of a port at once.

study.title: Driving an LED
study.body: An LED drops roughly its forward voltage $V_F$ (red ≈ 1.8 V, green ≈ 2.1 V, blue/white ≈ 3 V) almost regardless of current, so a series resistor must set the current. The resistor takes the rest of the pin voltage. Choose $I_F$ well below the pin's current limit. Example: 3.3 V pin, red LED, 10 mA: $R$ = (3.3 − 1.8)/0.01 = 150 Ω.

study.title: Pull-up and pull-down resistors
study.body: A switch to ground with a **pull-up** resistor to $V_{DD}$ gives a defined level in both positions: open: the pin reads 1 (no current, no drop across $R_{pu}$), closed: the pin reads 0 (**active low**). A pull-down to ground with the switch to $V_{DD}$ gives active-high. While the switch is closed a current $V_{DD}/R_{pu}$ flows, so values of 4.7–100 kΩ are used. Most microcontrollers have switchable internal pull-ups (≈ 20–50 kΩ).

study.title: Switch bounce and debouncing
study.body: Mechanical contacts **bounce**: when a switch closes, the contact makes and breaks several times for up to a few milliseconds, so a fast input sees several presses. Remedies: an RC filter followed by a Schmitt-trigger input, an SR latch with a changeover switch, or software (after a change, wait about 10–20 ms, or accept a new level only when several samples in a row agree).

study.title: Timers and PWM
study.body: A **timer** is a counter clocked by $f_{clk}$ divided by a prescaler $N$; it counts up to TOP (or overflows at $2^n$) and can raise an interrupt or toggle a pin. **PWM** switches an output on for $t_{on}$ in every period $T$; the duty cycle $D = t_{on}/T$ sets the average voltage, which a motor, a heater or an LED (via the eye) averages out. Changing the PWM frequency does not change the average, only the ripple. Drag $D$: the average (dashed) is $D V_H$. Drag the time constant of an RC low-pass after the pin (PWM period 1 ms): the filtered voltage (blue) ripples around the same average, less as $RC$ grows, but it then also follows changes of $D$ more slowly.

study.title: Serial interfaces: UART, SPI, I²C
study.body: **UART**: asynchronous, one TX and one RX line, no clock; each byte is framed by a start bit (0) and a stop bit (1) and sent LSB first at an agreed **baud rate** (8N1: 10 bits per byte). **SPI**: synchronous, the master drives SCLK, MOSI and a select line per slave and reads MISO; full duplex and fast (MHz). **I²C**: two open-drain lines SDA and SCL with pull-up resistors, devices chosen by a 7-bit address, every byte acknowledged (9 clocks per byte).

steps.title: General-purpose I/O pins
steps.body: Most microcontroller pins are **GPIO**: the program decides whether a pin is an input or an output. An output pin behaves like a voltage source of about $V_{DD}$ (logic 1) or 0 V (logic 0) with a limited current capability (typically 5–20 mA). An input pin draws almost no current and just reads whether the voltage is high or low.

steps.prompt: A GPIO pin ($V_{OH}$ = {{VOH|V}}) drives an LED with $V_F$ = {{VF|V}} through a series resistor. Which resistance gives an LED current of {{I|A}}?
steps.explanation: The resistor takes the voltage the LED does not: $V_R = V_{OH} - V_F$ = {{VOH|V}} − {{VF|V}} = {{VOH-VF|V}}. Then $R = V_R / I$ = {{VOH-VF|V}} / {{I|A}} = **{{(VOH-VF)/I|Ω}}** (pick the next standard value).

steps.prompt: What happens if an LED is connected straight from an output pin to ground, without a series resistor?
options: The current is limited only by the pin's internal resistance: it can exceed the pin rating and damage the pin or LED
Nothing: the LED takes exactly its rated current
The LED does not light because there is no resistor
The pin automatically switches to input mode
steps.explanation: An LED's current rises steeply once its voltage exceeds $V_F$. Without a resistor nothing sets the current except the small output resistance of the pin, so the current can be far above the 5–20 mA a pin is rated for.

steps.title: Pull-up resistors
steps.body: A pushbutton between an input pin and ground is not enough: while it is open, the pin would **float** and read random values. A **pull-up** resistor to $V_{DD}$ fixes this. Open: no current, so the pin is at $V_{DD}$ (logic 1). Pressed: the switch connects the pin to ground (logic 0). Such an input is called **active low**.

steps.prompt: In the pull-up circuit the button is **pressed**. What logic level does the program read on the pin?
steps.explanation: The closed switch connects the pin directly to ground, so it reads 0. The pull-up resistor now just carries a current $V_{DD}/R_{pu}$. When the button is released the resistor pulls the pin back up to 1.

steps.prompt: A pull-up of {{R|Ω}} to {{V|V}} is used with a pushbutton to ground. What current flows while the button is pressed?
steps.explanation: With the switch closed the whole supply voltage is across $R_{pu}$: $I = V_{DD}/R_{pu}$ = {{V|V}} / {{R|Ω}} = **{{V/R|A}}**. The input pin itself draws practically nothing. A larger $R_{pu}$ saves power but makes the input more sensitive to noise.

steps.title: Switch bounce
steps.body: When a mechanical switch closes, its contacts **bounce** several times before they settle, typically within a few milliseconds. A microcontroller samples so fast that it would see several presses. **Debouncing** removes this: in hardware with an RC filter and a Schmitt trigger, or in software by waiting 10–20 ms after a change before accepting the new level.

steps.prompt: Without debouncing, a program that counts button presses on every falling edge may count one press several times.
steps.explanation: True. Every bounce produces another falling edge, so one press can be counted 2, 3 or more times. Debouncing makes sure a single press gives a single clean transition.

steps.prompt: A PWM signal switches between 0 and {{V|V}} with a duty cycle of {{D}} %. What is its average voltage?
steps.explanation: The signal is high for {{D}} % of each period, so $V_{avg} = D \cdot V_H$ = {{D/100}} × {{V|V}} = **{{D/100*V|V}}**.

steps.prompt: The graph shows a PWM output (period 1 ms).

ask.explanation: The signal is high for $t_{on}$ = {{D}} ms in every period $T$ = 1 ms: $D = t_{on}/T$ = **{{100*D|%}}**.
High level {{VH|V}}, on for {{D}} ms of each 1 ms: $D$ = {{100*D|%}}, so $V_{avg} = D V_H$ = {{D}} × {{VH|V}} = **{{D*VH|V}}**.

steps.prompt: A motor driver is switched by PWM at {{f|Hz}} with an on-time of {{ton|s}} per period, from a {{V|V}} supply. What average voltage does the motor see?

A 5 V, 1 kHz PWM output with $D$ = {{D}} feeds an RC low-pass to make a simple DAC. Choose the **smallest** time constant $RC$ that keeps the peak-to-peak ripple within {{X}} mV (between the orange lines). A larger $RC$ would only slow the DAC down.
steps.hint: For $RC \gg T$ the capacitor charges almost linearly: $\Delta v \approx \frac{(V_H - \bar v)\,DT}{RC}$ with $\bar v = DV_H$.
steps.explanation: While the output is high the capacitor charges with current $(V_H - \bar v)/R$ for $DT$; with $RC \gg T$ the voltage changes almost linearly, so $\Delta v \approx \frac{V_H(1-D)\,DT}{RC}$. Setting $\Delta v$ = {{X}} mV: $RC = \frac{5 \cdot {{D}} \cdot {{1-D}} \cdot 1\,\text{ms}}{ {{X/1000}}\,\text{V} }$ = {{tau0/1000|s}}. The ripple is worst at $D = 0.5$; the price of a large $RC$ is a slow response: after a change of $D$ the output needs about $5RC$ = {{5*tau0/1000|s}} to settle.

steps.prompt: A timer runs from $f_{clk}$ = {{fc|Hz}} with prescaler $N$ = {{N}} and counts from 0 to TOP = {{TOP||4}}, then restarts. It generates one PWM period per count cycle. What is the PWM frequency?
steps.explanation: One count cycle has TOP + 1 = {{TOP+1}} ticks of {{N}}/{{fc|Hz}} each: $f_{PWM} = f_{clk}/(N(\text{TOP}+1))$ = {{fc|Hz}} / ({{N}} × {{TOP+1}}) = **{{fc/(N*(TOP+1))|Hz}}**. (Forgetting the +1 is a classic off-by-one error.)

steps.prompt: An {{n}}-bit timer is clocked at {{fc|Hz}} through a prescaler of {{N}}. How long does it take from 0 until it overflows?
steps.explanation: Tick = $N/f_{clk}$ = {{N}}/{{fc|Hz}} = {{N/fc|s}}. The counter overflows after $2^{ {{n}} }$ = {{2^n||5}} ticks: $T$ = {{2^n||5}} × {{N/fc|s}} = **{{2^n*N/fc|s}}**.

steps.prompt: A timer is clocked at {{fc|Hz}} through a prescaler of {{N}}. How many timer ticks must it count for an interval of {{t|s}}?
steps.explanation: Timer clock = {{fc|Hz}} / {{N}} = {{fc/N|Hz}}, i.e. one tick every {{N/fc|s}}. Ticks = {{t|s}} × {{fc/N|Hz}} = **{{t*fc/N||5}}**. (If it must fit in an 8-bit timer, it has to be ≤ 256; otherwise choose a larger prescaler.)

steps.prompt: Which graph shows a PWM signal with a duty cycle of {{100*D|%}} and a period of 1 ms?
steps.explanation: Duty cycle = on-time / period. The right graph repeats every 1 ms (ticks at 1 ms) and is high for {{D}} ms of each period. The inverted one has $D$ = {{100*(1-D)|%}}; the one with the same on-time but a 2 ms period has $D$ = {{50*D|%}}.

steps.prompt: An {{n}}-bit PWM ($2^{ {{n}} }$ duty-cycle steps) drives an RC low-pass filter from a {{V|V}} output to make a simple D/A converter. What is the smallest step in the average output voltage?
steps.explanation: The duty cycle can be set in steps of $1/2^{ {{n}} }$ = 1/{{2^n||5}}, so the average voltage changes in steps of $V_H/2^n$ = {{V|V}} / {{2^n||5}} = **{{V/2^n|V}}**.

steps.prompt: Doubling the PWM frequency while keeping the duty cycle the same doubles the average output voltage.
steps.explanation: False. $V_{avg} = D V_H$ depends only on the duty cycle. A higher frequency only makes the ripple after filtering (or in a motor's current) smaller, at the cost of more switching losses.

steps.prompt: A debounce filter: when the button is released, a capacitor $C$ = {{C|F}} charges from 0 V towards $V_{DD}$ = 5 V through $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. The Schmitt-trigger input switches when the capacitor reaches {{VT|V}}. How long after the release does the input switch?
steps.explanation: $v_C(t) = V_{DD}(1 - e^{-t/RC})$. Setting $v_C = V_T$: $t = RC\,\ln\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{DD} - V_T}$. $RC$ = {{R|Ω}} × {{C|F}} = {{R*C|s}}, so $t$ = {{R*C|s}} × ln(5/{{5-VT}}) = **{{R*C*ln(5/(5-VT))|s}}**. Bounces shorter than this are filtered out.

steps.prompt: Match each serial interface to its signals.
pairs: TX and RX, no clock line
SCLK, MOSI, MISO and a select per slave
SDA and SCL with pull-up resistors
steps.explanation: UART is asynchronous: both sides agree on the baud rate and resynchronise on every start bit. SPI and I²C are synchronous: the master supplies a clock. SPI uses separate data lines in each direction plus one select line per slave; I²C shares two open-drain lines between all devices and selects them by address.

steps.prompt: The graph shows one UART frame on the TX line (idle high, 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit). Remember that UART sends the **LSB first**. What byte is sent, as a decimal number?
steps.explanation: After the start bit (low) come $b_0 \ldots b_7$ in order: {{b0}}, {{b1}}, {{b2}}, {{b3}}, {{b4}}, {{b5}}, {{b6}}, {{b7}}. Written MSB first that is {{b7}}{{b6}}{{b5}}{{b4}} {{b3}}{{b2}}{{b1}}{{b0}} = **{{1*b0 + 2*b1 + 4*b2 + 8*b3 + 16*b4 + 32*b5 + 64*b6 + 128*b7}}**. Reading the bits in the order they appear as MSB-first is the classic mistake.

steps.prompt: A UART sends frames with 1 start bit, 8 data bits, {{p}} parity bit(s) and {{s}} stop bit(s) at {{baud||6}} baud, back to back.

ask.prompt: How many data bytes per second does it transfer?
ask.explanation: Each byte needs 1 + 8 + {{p}} + {{s}} = {{9+p+s}} bit periods. Bytes/s = {{baud||6}} / {{9+p+s}} = **{{baud/(9+p+s)||4}}**.

ask.prompt: How long does it take to send {{N}} bytes?

steps.prompt: A UART with 16× oversampling uses baud rate = $f_{clk}/(16 \cdot \text{DIV})$, with an integer divisor DIV. The clock is {{fc|Hz}} and the target is {{baud||6}} baud.

ask.prompt: Which divisor DIV gives the closest baud rate?
With the best integer divisor, what is the size of the baud-rate error (in %)?
ask.explanation: DIV = round({{fc/(16*baud)||4}}) = {{div}}. Actual rate = {{fc|Hz}} / (16 × {{div}}) = {{act||5}} baud. Error = |{{act||5}} − {{baud||6}}| / {{baud||6}} = **{{100*abs(act-baud)/baud|%}}**. Errors above about 2 % make reception unreliable, which is why crystals like 14.7456 MHz exist.

steps.prompt: An SPI master clocks out {{N}} bytes at an SCLK of {{f|Hz}} (one bit per clock, no gaps). How long does the transfer take?
steps.explanation: {{N}} bytes × 8 = {{8*N||5}} bits, one per clock: $t$ = {{8*N||5}} / {{f|Hz}} = **{{8*N/f|s}}**. During the same clocks the slave sends {{N}} bytes back on MISO (full duplex).

steps.prompt: An I²C master writes {{N}} data byte(s) to a sensor at SCL = {{f|Hz}}. Every byte, including the address byte, takes 9 clock cycles (8 bits + ACK). Ignoring the start and stop conditions, how long does the transaction take?
steps.explanation: Address byte + {{N}} data byte(s) = {{N+1}} bytes × 9 clocks = {{9*(N+1)}} clocks. $t$ = {{9*(N+1)}} / {{f|Hz}} = **{{9*(N+1)/f|s}}**.

steps.prompt: Why do the SDA and SCL lines of an I²C bus need pull-up resistors?
options: The outputs are open-drain: devices can only pull a line low, so the resistor makes it high
To limit the current into the microcontroller inputs
To terminate the line and prevent reflections
steps.explanation: Every I²C device drives the lines with open-drain transistors that can only pull them low. A line is high only when nobody pulls it down, via the pull-up. This wired-AND lets several devices share the lines without short circuits, and makes ACK and clock stretching possible.

steps.prompt: The rise time (30 %–70 %) of an I²C line is $t_r \approx 0.85\,R_pC_b$. The bus capacitance is {{C|F}} and the maximum allowed rise time is {{tr|s}}. What is the largest pull-up resistance $R_p$ you can use?
steps.explanation: $R_p \le t_r/(0.85\,C_b)$ = {{tr|s}} / (0.85 × {{C|F}}) = **{{tr/(0.85*C)|Ω}}**. A larger resistor makes edges too slow; a much smaller one draws more current than the open-drain outputs may sink (3 mA in standard mode).

steps.prompt: You must connect ten sensors to a microcontroller using only two signal wires, each sensor having its own address. Which interface fits?
steps.explanation: I²C shares two lines (SDA, SCL) between up to about a hundred devices, each selected by its address. SPI would need a separate select line for every sensor, UART is point-to-point, and PWM is not a data bus.
